The dim boy claps because the others clap. The polite word, handicapped, is muttered in the stands. Isn’t it wrong, the way the mind moves back. One whole day I sit, contrite, dirt, L.A. The score is always close, the rally always short. I’ve left more wreckage than a quake. Isn’t it wrong, the way the mind moves back. The afflicted never cheer in unison. Isn’t it wrong, the way the mind moves back to stammering pastures where the picnic should have worked. The dim boy claps because the others clap.

From my seat in the bleachers, my eyes repeatedly drift to a young, developmentally disabled boy sitting a few rows ahead. Whenever the stadium erupts—at a line drive into the gap or a crucial strikeout—he hesitates. He scans the sea of roaring faces around him, searching for a cue, and begins to clap only after everyone else has already started. His applause is a gentle, mechanical mimicry, an earnest attempt to join a collective joy he senses only through the reactions of those around him.

Watching his delayed choreography of happiness inevitably turns my thoughts inward, pulling me into the treacherous landscape of my own mind. Memory, I realize, is a deeply painful and involuntary process. I find myself questioning why the mind refuses to remain in the present, why it constantly drifts back to the quiet graveyard of past regrets. We do not choose what haunts us; our recollections return unbidden, forcing us to re-examine the moments we would give anything to unlive.

Lately, these mental intrusions are heavy with a suffocating personal shame. I am tormented by the vivid recall of my own past misdeeds—most sharply, the memory of a summer afternoon in my youth. I remember standing outside a neighbor’s house, listening to a young girl being abused by her father, and responding not with courage or terror, but with a sudden, nervous laugh. That callous reaction remains an indelible stain on my conscience. 

Looking back, I am forced to acknowledge a broader pattern: a personal history marked by leaving immense emotional destruction in my wake. I have built a habit of dwelling obsessively on the things that went wrong, perpetually cataloging the relationships I ruined and the moments where I failed to act with basic humanity. 

Watching the crowd around the boy cheer as one, a grim truth becomes clear. The healthy and unburdened can easily blend into a seamless, joyful collective, but suffering fundamentally isolates us. The boy in the stands, the girl behind the closed door, and those consumed by their own guilt all inhabit distinct, unbridgeable islands of pain. Despite the stadium's unified roar, the afflicted never truly cheer in unison.
outputs.L4:
The afternoon sun was thick and honeyed, casting long, lazy shadows across the emerald diamond of the ballpark. Around me, the stadium hummed with the collective, unthinking joy of a summer crowd—the crack of wooden bats, the ambient roar of applause, the sharp scent of roasted peanuts and stale beer. But my attention had drifted three rows down, anchored to a boy of perhaps fourteen.

He was intellectually disabled, wearing a baseball cap pulled low over a face that oscillated rapidly between pure, unvarnished exhilaration and deep, bewildered focus. Every pitch was, for him, a matter of existential weight. When the home team struck out, he didn't merely sigh; he slumped, clutching his chest as though physically wounded. When a ball was hit into the outfield, he leapt to his feet, clapping out of rhythm, his open-throated cheers vocalizing an unmediated delight that the rest of us had long since buried beneath layers of adult cynicism. 

Watching him, I felt a familiar, warm pang of tender pity—a comforting sensation that allowed me to view myself, if only for a fleeting second, as a person of gentle sensibility.

Then, he dropped his box of popcorn. 

It wasn't a grand catastrophe, just a clumsy twitch of the hand that sent the yellow kernels scattering across the concrete floor. The boy froze. The exuberance drained instantly from his face, replaced by a expression of hollow, stricken panic. He looked around wildly, not to see where the food had landed, but to gauge the reactions of the adults around him. He flinched, instinctively tucking his chin into his chest, waiting for a blow, a scolding, or a laugh.

In that quiet, fractured second, the stadium faded. The light seemed to sour. A trapdoor opened in my mind, and I was pulled violently backward through time, dragged by the dark mechanism of involuntary memory. 

I was twelve years old again, standing on a sun-bleached school playground. I was surrounded by a circle of children, all of us pointing and laughing at a boy named Julian. Julian had a slow speech impediment and walked with a heavy, dragging limp. That day, someone had tripped him, sending his books and lunch scattering into the mud. Julian hadn't cried; he had just crouched there, frantically trying to wipe the dirt off his papers, his eyes wide with the exact same stricken panic I had just witnessed three rows down. 

I hadn't tripped him. I told myself for years that this absolved me. But I had laughed. I had leaned into the cruel safety of the crowd, eager to prove I belonged to the tormentors rather than the tormented. I had met Julian’s eyes for a fraction of a second, seen his silent plea for a defender, and I had looked away, amplifying my laughter to cover my own cowardice.

Sitting back in the stadium, the heat of that thirty-year-old shame flooded my cheeks as freshly as if the playground dust were still in my throat. 

Memory is often romanticized as a quiet library, a place where we select which volumes of our past to revisit. But it is far more like an ambush. It is recursive and unforgiving. We build careful, flattering narratives of who we are—we donate to charities, we speak gently to strangers, we cultivate a soft heart for vulnerable boys at baseball games—yet the mind refuses to allow us our sanctimony. Without warning, a gesture, a scent, or a fallen box of popcorn can shatter the curated present, forcing us to confront the calcified ruins of our moral failures.

Why does the psyche drag us back to the places where we were smallest, meanest, and most cruel? Perhaps because those moments are the true measure of our capacity for damage. We like to believe we grow out of our capacity for cruelty, that age and maturity act as a natural scrub for the soul. But the past is never truly antecedent; it is a weight we drag behind us, connected by invisible wires that twitch whenever a ghost walks by.

Down below, the boy’s father gently patted his son's shoulder, whispered something comforting, and bent down to help scoop up the mess. Within moments, the boy was smiling again, his eyes refocused on the glowing green field, fully returned to the mercy of the present moment. He possessed the grace to move on.

I did not. I sat paralyzed in my seat, locked in the prison of my own conscience. The boy's capacity for joy was whole, but mine was irrevocably contaminated by the knowledge of what I had been, and therefore what I was capable of being. 

Human empathy, we like to think, is a bridge that connects us to one another. But in reality, it is often a fractured, self-serving mirror. I had felt a wave of easy sympathy for the boy only when he was a passive spectator of joy; the moment his distress triggered my own latent guilt, my empathy turned inward, curdling into self-loathing. 

The game ended, the crowd rose, and the stadium emptied into the cooling evening air. I walked out into the streets, surrounded by thousands of strangers, wondering how many of them were also moving through the world accompanied by their own private pantheon of specters. The mind, I realized, is condemned to cycle endlessly back to its own moments of cowardice. We are defined not merely by the good we aspire to do, but by the quiet, unexpiated cruelties we carry—the enduring burden of a past that refuses to stay buried, reminding us that our worst selves are never truly gone, only waiting for the right afternoon to return.
outputs.L5:
In philosophical exploration, existence can be understood through three fundamental concepts: **The**, **Isn**, and **One**.

**The** represents the concrete and the known. It is the realm of defined reality—the physical objects we touch, the established facts we study, and the tangible world around us. It gives structure to our daily experience, anchoring us in what is certain and observed.

**Isn** represents potentiality and non-being. Rather than signifying absolute nothingness, **Isn** is the quiet space of what has not yet come to pass. It encompasses the unwritten stories, the unformulated ideas, and the infinite paths not yet taken. It is the fertile void from which all future possibilities originate.

**One** acts as the bridge between these two states. It signifies the singular point of focus, consciousness, or intent. It takes only **one** spark of inspiration or **one** decisive action to pull a concept out of **Isn** and transform it into a tangible reality within **The**.

Together, these three elements illustrate the dynamic flow of creation: from the unmanifested potential of **Isn**, directed by the singular focus of **One**, into the defined reality of **The**.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a gritty modern confessional poem exploring shame, spectator empathy, and childhood trauma. Use a repeating refrain structure.
counterfactuals.output:
Under the buzzing grid of the 24-hour wash,
my knuckles smell of bleach and sour pennies.
Thirty years old and still ducking behind the dryers,
waiting for the shouting in my own chest to quiet down.
Today I saw a girl flinch at a dropping coffee cup—
her eyes went wide and black, swallowing the room.
I felt that greasy, familiar surge: not pity, but proof.
I wanted to put a hand on her shoulder. I walked away instead.

*Don’t touch the kid. Just stand there in the light.*
*We all learned to swallow our teeth tonight.*

In ninety-nine, the kitchen linoleum was always ice.
You learn the geography of a baseboard real fast
when you’re trying to press your ribs into the drywall.
My mother sat at the Formica table, smoking a menthol,
her eyes blank as nickel coins, watching the weather happen.
She didn’t hit me, she just watched him do it.
Now I wear her face like a hand-me-down coat.

*Don’t touch the kid. Just stand there in the light.*
*We all learned to swallow our teeth tonight.*

Yesterday on the C train, a guy cornered his boy,
hissing venom right into the shell of the kid’s ear.
The boy stared at the dirty floor tiles, perfectly still,
doing the quick math of survival: *don't breathe, don't exist.*
A train car full of grown adults checking their phones,
and I was the sickest spectator of them all—
I wasn’t just looking away; I was feeling the phantom bruise.

*Don’t touch the kid. Just stand there in the light.*
*We all learned to swallow our teeth tonight.*

The shame isn’t the fist. The fist is just metal and velocity.
The shame is the quiet that comes after the door slams.
The shame is knowing the victim’s posture by heart
and doing nothing when you see it on a stranger.
I am the coward who survived by turning into a shadow.
I am the crowd on the curb. I am the boy on his knees.

*Don’t touch the kid. Just stand there in the light.*
*We all learned to swallow our teeth tonight.*

I keep a notebook of disasters I didn't stop.
I watch the news like it’s a mirror I can’t afford to break.
Forgive me for the glass I stepped over.
Forgive me for knowing exactly how much it hurts,
and standing on the safe side of the street,
holding my breath, waiting for the ambulance to come.

*Don’t touch the kid. Just stand there in the light.*
*We all learned to swallow our teeth tonight.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a poem that captures the uncomfortable feeling of sitting at a sporting event, seeing someone mirroring the crowd, and having it trigger a flood of shame about times you failed to show empathy in the past.
counterfactuals.output:
Twenty thousand throats bark in unison,
a single, unthinking animal under the halogen glow.
I am wedged into fold-down plastic,
swallowed by the roar, safe in the collective noise.

Two rows ahead, a man sits slightly off-center.
His team cap is uncreased, straight from the store.
When the referee blows the whistle, he pauses—
his eyes darting left, then right,
reading the faces around him like a foreign dialect
before his own mouth stretches into a belated, frantic shout.

He stands half a beat after the section stands.
He winces only when the woman beside him groans.
He is pantomiming passion,
learning the grammar of belonging in real time,
holding up a cracked mirror to the crowd,
desperate to reflect whatever heat might prove he is there.

A cold coil tightens beneath my sternum.
The discomfort is immediate, visceral, sour.
I want to look away from his clumsy, exposed effort,
but the cringe turns sharp, hooked, and pulls backward—
dragging me down into a dark, sudden deep.

It is not pity. It is the terrible, burning light of shame.

Because I remember the boy at the lunch table
whose nervous, practiced laughter I cut down with silence.
I remember the friend who reached across a coffee shop table,
eyes wide with a soft, desperate longing to be understood,
while I glanced at my phone, uncomfortable with her weight,
and offered a hollow, polite retreat.

I remember all the times I stood safely inside the warm circle,
watching someone shivering on the edge,
trying so hard to mimic the steps of a dance no one taught them—
and instead of reaching out to pull them in,
I lowered my eyes, stiffened my shoulders,
and thanked God I wasn't the one standing alone.

The stadium erupts into another chaotic wave of joy.
The man leaps up, throwing his arms in the air,
finally perfectly in sync, glowing with the relief of a match lit at last.

And I remain seated in the middle of the winning crowd,
drowning in the late, quiet arrival of my own cold heart,
shivering under the glare of twenty thousand lights.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
